equivalent: The guard is a PUSH-time filter for a condition that is also checked at POP time: the loop's first act on a popped arrival is 'if first_spike[v].is_some() { continue }'. Dropping it therefore adds only entries that are discarded when they come out, and it adds none for a vertex that has not fired -- at push time an unfired w passes both spellings. Nothing else moves: syn_events is incremented and the arrival time is checked for overflow BEFORE the guard, and BinaryHeap pops the minimum of a total order on (tick, presynaptic index, vertex), so consuming extra minima that are immediately skipped cannot reorder the entries that remain. Every field of Wavefront -- first_spike, parent, spikes, syn_events, ticks -- and every path_to are therefore unchanged; what changes is the heap's size, which no caller can observe. Measured, not asserted: a fixture running wavefront from EVERY source of 40 seeded random graphs of 3 to 14 vertices at 45% density, with duplicate edges and self-loops, plus path_to for every vertex -- 5160 printed lines -- is byte-identical under both spellings.

old: let (a, b) = (k as f64, (n - k) as f64);
new: let (a, b) = ((n - k) as f64, k as f64);
equivalent: The expression a*b*(a*a + b*b - 2.0)/3.0 is SYMMETRIC in a and b, and the guard above it (n == 0 || k > n -> None) is what makes n - k well defined, so both spellings compute the same two numbers and combine them the same way. In f64 this is bit-exact and not merely mathematically equal: IEEE-754 multiplication and addition are commutative on non-NaN operands -- a*b and b*a round the same exact product, a*a + b*b and b*b + a*a round the same exact sum -- so no rounding can distinguish them. Measured, not asserted: ruin_steps_variance printed as raw bit patterns for every (k, n) with n < 40 and k <= 42, including the None cases, is byte-identical under both spellings.
